nameStory: The Atlantic Argentine gets its name from its silvery, metallic appearance that reminded early fishermen of polished silver - 'argentine' comes from the Latin 'argentum' meaning silver. The 'Atlantic' part distinguishes it from similar silvery fish found in the Pacific Ocean. This deep-sea dweller truly lives up to its shimmering name when brought to the surface.
description: The Atlantic Argentine is a sleek, silvery fish that lives in the deep waters off New England's coast. This metallic beauty can grow quite large for a smelt-like fish, reaching over two feet in length. With its streamlined body and bright silver coloration, it's built for life in the ocean's middle depths. You're most likely to encounter one at a fish market or restaurant rather than while fishing from shore, as they live far offshore in very deep water.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant metallic silver sides that flash like polished chrome, with a darker back that appears almost blue-black when fresh

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated and torpedo-shaped with a compressed body that feels firm and muscular to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Much larger than typical smelts, reaching up to 27 inches long - about the size of a decent trout

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small mouth positioned at the front tip of the head (terminal), with tiny teeth that feel like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small adipose fin (fleshy fin without rays) behind the dorsal fin, characteristic of the smelt family

habitat: Atlantic Argentines live in the deep, cold waters of the continental shelf and slope off New England's coast, typically at depths between 460 and 4,700 feet. They prefer the open ocean environment far from shore, swimming in schools in the dark, frigid waters above the ocean floor. These fish are only encountered by commercial fishing vessels using deep-water trawls or occasionally brought up by deep-sea fishing charters.

seasonality.spring: Commercial fishing vessels may encounter schools as they begin seasonal movements in deeper offshore waters.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for commercial harvest, when schools are more concentrated and easier to locate in deep waters.
seasonality.fall: Continues to be available to commercial fisheries, with fish often in prime condition before winter.
seasonality.winter: Less commonly encountered due to challenging fishing conditions in deep offshore waters during winter storms.

funFact: Despite being called a 'smelt,' Atlantic Argentines can grow to nearly 28 inches long - that's bigger than many salmon and almost ten times the size of the rainbow smelt most New Englanders know!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large rainbow smelt or small Atlantic herring due to the silvery coloration. Look for the small adipose fin behind the dorsal fin (herring don't have this) and the much larger size compared to typical smelts. The firm, muscular body texture also distinguishes it from the softer feel of most herring.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'smelt' can be confusing here, as most people think of smelts as small fish you can eat whole, but Atlantic Argentines are substantial fish that are filleted like larger species. They're also called 'greater silver smelt' in some markets, which better reflects their impressive size compared to other smelt species.
compareHints: As the only Argentina species regularly found in New England waters, compare it to other members of the broader smelt family. Unlike rainbow smelt which are much smaller and often found in coastal waters, Atlantic Argentines are exclusively deep-water fish with a more robust build. They lack the cucumber scent that fresh rainbow smelt are famous for, instead having a clean, ocean smell typical of deep-water fish.
